Task T1: What does multiplying a graph mean?

0. Input and Code

Input is HW8_graph_data.json exported by the course notebook: the base mini-web (12 vertices, 23 weighted edges) and cluster_graph(n, seed=8) for n = 64, 128, 256, 512. Node order is the notebook's order, so row i and column i are node i. Rows are sources, columns are destinations. The weights are ignored in T1: A[i][j] = 1 exactly when the edge i → j exists.

All algorithms are my own Rust code: matrix products, Warshall, Boolean repeated squaring, BFS and SCC grouping are in src/lib.rs, the experiment is src/bin/T1.rs and the figures are drawn with the plotters crate (src/draw.rs). Python is used only for checking: hw8_check.py imports the course helpers, runs check_closure on every closure, compares A², A³ with NumPy and the SCCs with NetworkX, and times two NumPy versions as a reference.

1. A² and A³ Count Walks

In the ordinary integer product, (A·A)[i][j] = Σk A[i][k]·A[k][j] adds 1 for every middle vertex k with edges i → k → j, so A²[i][j] is the number of walks of length 2 from i to j, and by the same argument A³[i][j] is the number of walks of length 3. The products are computed with 64-bit integers.

Three-hop check, 0 Home → 4 Graphs

All walks 0 → a → b → 4 were listed by checking every pair (a, b) with edges 0 → a, a → b, b → 4:

#WalkPagesSimple path?
1[0, 1, 2, 4]0 Home → 1 Courses → 2 Algorithms → 4 Graphsyes
2[0, 1, 3, 4]0 Home → 1 Courses → 3 Trees → 4 Graphsyes

2 walks were found and A³[0][4] = 2, so the count matches the matrix entry. Here both walks happen to be simple paths. That is not true in general: for 1 Courses → 4 Graphs, A³[1][4] = 3 and one of the three walks goes around the cycle 1 ⇄ 4:

WalkPagesSimple path?
[1, 2, 3, 4]1 Courses → 2 Algorithms → 3 Trees → 4 Graphsyes
[1, 3, 2, 4]1 Courses → 3 Trees → 2 Algorithms → 4 Graphsyes
[1, 4, 1, 4]1 Courses → 4 Graphs → 1 Courses → 4 Graphsno (revisits 1, 4)

So matrix powers count walks, which may repeat vertices and edges, not simple paths.

2. Reflexive Transitive Closure, Two Ways

R[i][j] is true when j can be reached from i by a path of length 0 or more, so the diagonal is always true. Both methods start from I ∨ A and use only OR/AND, never unbounded walk counts:

  • Warshall: for k = 0 … n−1, for every i with R[i][k] true, set row i to row i OR row k. After step k, R[i][j] says whether there is a path whose intermediate vertices are all in {0, …, k}. One pass over all k gives the closure.
  • Repeated squaring: R ← R ⊙ R with the Boolean product (R ⊙ R)[i][j] = ORk (R[i][k] AND R[k][j]). If R covers paths of length ≤ L, the square covers ≤ 2L, so after s squarings all paths of length ≤ 2s are included. The loop stops when a squaring does not change the matrix; that last squaring is counted.

On the mini-web the longest shortest path is 5 edges (1 Courses → 4 → 5 → 6 → 8 → 11 Exit). Squaring covers lengths 2, 4, 8, so it changes the matrix three times and the fourth squaring confirms: 4 squarings. Each method was implemented twice in Rust: with bit rows (one u64 holds 64 entries) and with plain bool entries. All four results are identical, equal the BFS reachability from every vertex, and have a true diagonal.

The closure has 89 true entries out of 144. Its block shape already shows the structure: Home reaches everything, the "course" pages 1–4 reach the research part 5–8, the research part reaches the partners and Exit, but nothing goes back. 9 and 10 reach only each other, and Exit reaches only itself.

true / count added at this step selected cell (click any cell)

The widget recomputes the same matrices in JavaScript for the mini-web. Walks: choose k and click a cell to list the walks it counts. Warshall: each step allows one more intermediate vertex; orange cells are new. Repeated squaring: each step doubles the covered path length; the last step changes nothing and stops the loop.

3. Why One Multiplication or Checking Aⁿ > 0 Is Not Enough

  • One product (I ∨ A)² only covers paths of length ≤ 2. On the mini-web it has 58 true entries instead of 89; for example 0 Home → 6 Projects (length 2) is found, but 0 Home → 11 Exit (length 4) is not. A path may need up to n − 1 edges, so the products must be repeated.
  • Aⁿ > 0 asks for walks of exactly n steps, not "at most n". With n = 12 the Boolean A¹² has 85 true entries and misses (0, 0), (9, 10), (10, 9), (11, 11). (0, 0) and (11, 11) are missed because Home and Exit lie on no cycle, so no walk returns to them (reflexivity needs I). (9, 10) and (10, 9) are missed because the only way between Partner A and Partner B is the 2-cycle, so every walk between them has odd length and none has length 12. The closure needs I ∨ A ∨ A² ∨ … ∨ Aⁿ⁻¹, which is what (I ∨ A)2s gives.
  • Integer counts grow. If ordinary multiplication is used instead of OR/AND, the numbers of walks grow exponentially with the length, so a uint8 accumulator overflows (256 becomes 0, which would wrongly mean "unreachable"). Thresholding to 0/1 after every product, as the Boolean product does, avoids this.

The chain of 17 vertices is the worst case for squaring relative to its size: the path 0 → 16 has 16 edges, so it needs 24 = 16 and 4 changing squarings plus one confirming, 5 in total; the closure is the upper triangle including the diagonal. The two-cycle plus isolated vertex converges after 1 squaring (nothing changes: I ∨ A is already closed), and the isolated vertex 2 has only its own diagonal entry, which is why it must be present in the vertex list.

5. Mutually Reachable Groups (SCCs)

Vertices i and j are put in the same group when both R[i][j] and R[j][i] are true. Each group was compared with NetworkX strongly_connected_components.

Home and Exit are single-vertex groups: Home has no incoming edges and Exit has no outgoing edges. The closed pair Partner A ⇄ Partner B is a trap: once a walker enters it, it cannot leave, which matters for T2 and T3. In all four cluster graphs the closure gives exactly four groups of n/4 vertices, matching the four generator blocks; the links between blocks are one-way, so the closure is block upper-triangular:

6. Timing on cluster_graph(n, seed=8)

Each method was run three times on each size and the median is reported. Only the closure computation is timed: loading the JSON, building the graph, checking and plotting are outside the timer. The rule "after a run exceeds 5 s, skip that size and all larger ones for that method" was implemented, but it never triggered: the slowest Rust run took 2.55 s. The NumPy rows come from hw8_check.py on the same machine and are given only as a reference.

Squaring, bit rows0.100 ms (5 sq.)0.404 ms (5 sq.)1.787 ms (5 sq.)5.134 ms (5 sq.)
Squaring, scalar bool2.045 ms (5 sq.)15.808 ms (5 sq.)119.040 ms (5 sq.)2545.988 ms (5 sq.)
NumPy Warshall (np.outer, reference)4.763 ms15.450 ms43.948 ms151.866 ms
NumPy int64 R @ R, threshold (reference)6.137 ms (5 sq.)126.632 ms (5 sq.)2160.367 ms (5 sq.)9493.185 ms (5 sq.)

What is vectorised

  • Bit rows (Rust): a row is stored as ⌈n/64⌉ u64 words, and "row i OR row k" is done word by word, so one machine instruction handles 64 matrix entries (word-level parallelism). In the Boolean product the same row-OR is used for every k with R[i][k] true. These simple loops can additionally be auto-vectorised by the compiler, but I did not rely on it.
  • Scalar bool (Rust): one entry per operation. Squaring uses the textbook i, j, k loops with an early exit as soon as one k is found.
  • NumPy reference: Warshall loops over k in Python, but each step R |= np.outer(R[:, k], R[k]) is one vectorised C operation on all n² entries. The squaring uses R @ R on int64 and then > 0; NumPy's integer matrix product does not go to BLAS, so it is a slow C loop: 9493.185 ms at n = 512.

Fewer matrix operations does not mean less work

Repeated squaring needs only 5 "matrix operations" here, while Warshall needs n = 512 update rounds. But one Boolean product costs Θ(n³) (n² entries, each an OR over n terms), and a Warshall round costs only Θ(n²), so Warshall does about n³ work in total and squaring about 5·n³ (in general ⌈log₂(longest path)⌉ + 1 products). The measurements agree: at n = 512 squaring with bit rows is 4.3× slower than Warshall with bit rows, and the scalar versions differ by 18.8×. Warshall also skips every row i with R[i][k] false, and the data layout matters more than the operation count: bit rows make Warshall 112× faster than the scalar version with the same algorithm. The scalar times grow by about 7–8× per doubling of n, as expected for n³. The bit-row times grow by only about 4× here, because with n ≤ 512 a row is at most 8 words, so the n/64 factor is still small next to the per-row overhead.

Task T2: Walkers versus a probability vector

0. Transition Matrix

P is built from the base mini-web by dividing each row of weights by its row sum, so P[i][j] = w(i → j) / Σk w(i → k). Exit (node 11) has no outgoing edges, so its row is set explicitly to 1/12 for every vertex: a walker standing on Exit jumps to a uniformly random vertex (possibly Exit itself). This is a rule for the dangling row only; every other row follows its links. For the comparison rule, "uniform among outgoing neighbours", every outgoing edge of a vertex gets the same probability and the Exit row stays the same. Both matrices are built in Rust (transition in src/lib.rs); every row sums to 1 and has no negative entries.

1. Simulator and Exact Vector

  • Simulation (Sampler in src/lib.rs, src/bin/T2.rs): each of the M walkers starts at 0 Home and makes exactly t transitions. A transition draws u uniformly from [0, 1) (SplitMix64) and takes the first destination whose cumulative row probability exceeds u. Only the final position of each walker is counted, not the vertices it visited on the way, and the counts are divided by M. Every walker is independent; every (rule, t, M) uses its own recorded seed.
  • Prediction: p0 = (1, 0, …, 0) for Home, and pt+1 = pt P (row vector times matrix), repeated t times. No matrix power is formed.
  • Error: L1 = Σv |empirical(v) − pt(v)|, which is between 0 and 2.

3. Comparison at t = 10

Both graphs use the same colour scale (0 to 0.33), so equal colours mean equal probabilities.

Which vertices gain or lose probability under weighted transitions?

  • Gain: Projects (+0.065), Research (+0.036), the course group 1–4 (together +0.084) and Updates. The heavy edges keep walkers inside the two groups: Home → Courses has weight 3 (3/4 instead of 1/2), so more walkers start in the course group, which can only be left through Graphs → Research; and Research → Projects has weight 4 (0.8 instead of 0.5), and from Projects about 61% of walkers are back at Research within two steps (1/3 directly, 1/6 via People, 1/9 via Updates).
  • Lose: Partner B (−0.167), Partner A (−0.042) and slightly People. Under the uniform rule Research sends half its walkers to People, and People sends half of those straight into Partner A, so the trap is reached faster: after 10 steps it holds 60.5% of the probability with the uniform rule but only 39.6% with weights.
  • Inside the trap the walkers alternate 9 → 10 → 9 every step. The split between Partner A and Partner B at t = 10 therefore depends on the parity of the step at which a walker entered (always at Partner A), so the two values are not equal and would swap roles at odd and even t.
  • Home keeps almost nothing (only walkers that jumped from Exit back to Home), and Exit stays small because it is reached only through Updates and is left immediately.

4. Does Increasing M Help?

To answer this without relying on one lucky or unlucky run, each (t, M) was repeated with 40 further seeds for M = 100, 300, 1,000, 3,000, 10,000, 30,000.

On average, yes: the error falls like 1/√M, so 10 times more walkers give about √10 ≈ 3.2 times smaller L1 (for t = 10 the mean goes from 0.0795 at M = 1,000 to 0.0245 at M = 10,000). But it is a statement about the average, not about every run. With the same seed index, M = 10,000 was better than M = 1,000 in 40/40 cases for t = 10 and 40/40 for t = 3, but only in 33/40 cases for t = 1. At t = 1 there are only two outcomes (Courses or Research), so the error is just 2·|share at Courses − 0.75| and a small sample can hit the 75 : 25 split exactly (the points on the bottom edge of the plot are runs with L1 = 0). Larger t spreads the probability over more vertices, so the L1 sum collects more small errors and is larger for the same M.

Task T3: Teleportation and PageRank

0. Model

The same weighted P as in T2 is used, with the uniform Exit row. Teleportation is applied as a vector update, without building any all-to-all matrix:

pk+1 = (1 − rho) · pk P + rho / n · (1, …, 1)

Since pk sums to 1, this is exactly "with probability rho jump to a uniformly random page, otherwise follow P". The start is p0 = all mass at Partner A (node 9). For rho > 0 the iteration stops when ||pk+1 − pk||1 < 10−10, or after 2,000 iterations (then it would be reported as not converged). Code: teleport_step, pagerank and long_walk in src/lib.rs, experiment src/bin/T3.rs.

1. rho = 0: Trapping and Oscillation

0 Home1 Courses2 Algorithms3 Trees4 Graphs5 Research6 Projects7 People8 Updates9 Partner A10 Partner B11 Exit
p0000000000100
p1000000000010
p2000000000100
p3000000000010
p4000000000100
p5000000000010

The six distributions p0 … p5 alternate between "everything at Partner A" and "everything at Partner B". Partner A has a single link to Partner B and Partner B a single link back, and T1 showed that {9, 10} is a closed SCC: nothing leaves it. So without teleportation

  • trapping: once mass is in {9, 10} it stays there forever (from any start, all mass would end up here, apart from mass still on its way);
  • oscillation: the cycle has period 2, so pk never settles. Every step changes the vector by L1 = 2. After 2,000 iterations the change is still 2: the iteration has not converged, and the final iterate (all mass at Partner A, because 2,000 is even) is not a stationary distribution. A stationary vector does exist (½ on each of 9 and 10), but power iteration from this start never reaches it.

All three positive values converge. The change shrinks by a factor of exactly (1 − rho) per step: the 2-cycle gives P an eigenvalue −1, which the teleportation step scales to −(1 − rho), and this is the slowest part to die out. That is why the iteration counts are almost exactly log(10−10/2) / log(1 − rho) (the grey numbers), and why rho = 0.05 needs about four times as many steps as rho = 0.20.

Effect of teleportation

  • It makes the chain escape the trap: from 9 and 10 a walker leaves with probability rho · 10/12 per step. The trap mass falls from 0.681 (rho = 0.05) to 0.521 and 0.368.
  • It removes the oscillation: some mass is always spread uniformly, so the period-2 behaviour is damped and there is a single stationary vector, the same for every start.
  • Larger rho makes the vector flatter (closer to 1/12 everywhere) and converge faster, but it also tells less about the links. Home stays lowest: no page links to it, so it only receives teleportation mass (rho/12) and the 1/12 share of the Exit row.
  • Partner A is above Partner B for every rho: Partner B is linked only from Partner A (π10 = rho/12 + (1 − rho)(π9 + π11/12)), while Partner A is also linked from People and Updates.

How could the trap be broken with as little change as possible? Bonus B1, section 4 tests every possible single new link out of {9, 10}: the best one (Partner A → Courses) leaves only 0.166 in the trap, the course's web_escape link Partner B → Home leaves 0.201.

5. Checks

  • All vectors are nonnegative and sum to 1 (check_distribution).
  • For rho = 0.05, 0.10, 0.20 on the mini-web and rho = 0.10 on clusters_256, check_pagerank (NetworkX with alpha = 1 − rho and uniform dangling rule) agrees within 10−8.
  • rho = 0 is not passed to the checker (it requires positive rho, and the iteration does not converge).

PageRank is not a universal measure of importance. Here the two partner pages rank highest only because they form a closed loop that keeps the walker; "Home", which every user would call the most important page, ranks lowest because nothing links to it. Changing rho, the weights, the dangling rule or one link (see web_escape) changes the ranking.

Task T4: A small flow problem: undoing a choice

0. Network

s → A, s → B (each student can be assigned once), A → X, A → Y, B → X (availability), X → t, Y → t (one seat each). Every capacity is 1, so a flow of value k is an assignment of k students. The trace below was done by hand first; the Rust program (src/bin/T4.rs, residual network FlowNet in src/lib.rs) then replays exactly these two paths, draws every step and confirms that no other choice was possible.

1. Hand Trace

  1. Augmentation 1: s → A → X → t, bottleneck 1 (panel 1 → 2). Student A takes session X. Value 1.
  2. Residual network after it (panel 3). For every original edge u → v with flow f and capacity c the residual network has u → v with c − f (if positive) and a reverse edge v → u with f (if positive). The used edges s → A, A → X, X → t are replaced by A → s, X → A, t → X. What remains forward: s → B, B → X, A → Y, Y → t.
  3. Augmentation 2: from s only B is reachable, from B only X, and from X only the reverse edge X → A; then A → Y → t. The unique augmenting path is s → B → X → A → Y → t, bottleneck 1 (the program enumerated all simple s–t paths in this residual network and found only this one). Value 2.
  4. Final residual network (panel 5): s has no outgoing residual edge, so t is unreachable and the flow is maximum.

What the reverse edge means

Traversing X → A cancels one unit of flow on A → X. In terms of people: B wants X, but X is taken by A; the path tells A to give up X and move to Y, which is free. The first decision (A in X) was not wrong forever, it is undone. Without reverse edges a greedy method would stop after the first path at value 1, with B unassigned.

2. Final Allocation and Certificate

Original edgeCapacityFlow
A → X10
A → Y11
B → X11
X → t11
Y → t11
s → A11
s → B11

Final assignment: A → Y, B → X, both students placed, flow value 2. The source side found by residual reachability is S = {s}; the cut edges are s -> A, s -> B, total capacity 2.

Why this proves optimality: every unit of flow from s to t has to cross from S to the other side through some cut edge, so any flow has value ≤ the capacity of any cut. We have a flow of value 2 and a cut of capacity 2, so no flow can be larger, and no cut can be smaller. (Here it is also obvious: only two students exist.) Checking all 16 cuts that separate s from t shows that the minimum capacity 2 is reached by five of them: {s}, {s, B}, {s, B, X}, {s, A, B, X}, {s, A, B, X, Y}.

Task T5: Enough seats, but can everyone attend?

0. Input

allocation_network(seed=8) unchanged: 200 students u000–u199, 12 sessions g00–g11, source s and sink t. Capacities: s → student 1, student → session 1 (an availability edge, not a preference), session → t = number of seats. The table shows, for every session, its seats, how many students can attend it, and (from the result below) how many were assigned.

There are exactly 200 seats for 200 students. But the generator gives u000–u059 (60 students) only g00 and g01 (40 seats together), and u060–u199 only sessions among g02–g11.

1. Edmonds–Karp

  • Residual network (FlowNet in src/lib.rs): every original edge u → v is stored as a forward arc with residual capacity c − f and a paired reverse arc v → u with residual f. Augmenting by δ subtracts δ from the arc used and adds δ to its partner, so forward and reverse capacities are always updated together.
  • Shortest augmenting path: BFS from s over arcs with positive residual capacity; the path is rebuilt from parent pointers, and the flow is increased by its bottleneck. Repeat until BFS no longer reaches t.
  • Minimum cut: after the last augmentation, S = vertices reachable from s in the residual network (reachable).
  • Counting convention for BFS edge examinations: when a vertex is taken from the queue, every arc in its adjacency list is counted once: forward and reverse arcs, including arcs with zero residual capacity and arcs to vertices already seen (unsuccessful tests). A BFS stops as soon as t is discovered. The final, unsuccessful BFS is included.

Validation on the T4 network: value 2 after 2 augmentations (24 examinations). BFS found exactly the hand-traced paths, s -> A -> X -> t and then s -> B -> X -> A -> Y -> t, and the residual reachability gives S = {s}. check_flow passes.

2. Three Runs

Each run starts from zero flow on a fresh copy of the network; only one session → t capacity is changed in the two experiments, no edges are added.

Every augmentation adds 1 (all bottlenecks are unit capacities), so the number of augmentations equals the number of assigned students. Most paths are the direct s → student → session → t; the longer ones (5 edges) go through a reverse edge and move an already assigned student to another session, as in T4. A BFS examines on average about 809 of the 1,504 residual arcs.

3. Why 20 Students Stay Unassigned: the Cut

The figure groups the 214 vertices into blocks; labels show summed flow/capacity, the yellow blocks are the source side S, red edges cross the cut. In the baseline S = {s, all 60 students u000–u059, g00, g01}. The edges leaving S are

  • s → u060 … u199: 140 edges of capacity 1, all used (all these students are assigned);
  • g00 → t and g01 → t: 20 + 20 seats, both full.

Total 180 = flow value, so 180 is the maximum. In words: 60 students can only use 40 seats, so at most 40 of them can be placed, whatever happens elsewhere. The other 140 students have 160 seats, so 20 seats in g02–g11 stay empty. The total capacity (200 seats for 200 students) hides this: seats in sessions that a student cannot attend do not help that student. Unassigned in the baseline: u040, u041, u042, u043, u044, u045, u046, u047, u048, u049, u050, u051, u052, u053, u054, u055, u056, u057, u058, u059.

4. Predictions and Experiments (+20 seats)

  • Prediction, g00 + 20 (should help): g00 is on the source side of the minimum cut and full; the 20 unassigned students can all attend g00. With 60 seats for the 60 restricted students the bottleneck disappears, so I predicted 200 assigned. Result: 200, no one unassigned. The new minimum cut is S = {s}: now the 200 edges s → student (the number of students) are the limit.
  • Prediction, g04 + 20 (should not help): g04 is full in the baseline (16/16), so "full session, add seats" looks tempting. But g04 is not on the source side: none of u000–u059 can attend it, and every student who can is already assigned (g10 and g11 still have free seats). Its full seat edge is not a cut edge, so I predicted no change. Result: 180, the same 20 unassigned and the same cut of 180. The flow is only rearranged: g04 now has 29/36, and other sessions among g02–g11 have correspondingly more empty seats.

Both predictions were correct, because they were made from the cut and not from the total number of seats: seats help only when added to a saturated cut edge. Adding the 20 seats to g01 instead of g00 would work the same way; adding them to any of g02–g11 would not.

5. Checks

  • In Rust and again in hw8_check.py for all three runs: every student has at most one assigned session, every assignment uses an existing availability edge, capacities and conservation hold, and flow value = cut capacity (check_flow on the modified copy of the network for the experiments).
  • NetworkX maximum_flow_value gives the same values: 180, 200, 180.
Bonus B1: Whose PageRank?

0. Personalised Teleportation

Same weighted P and rho = 0.10 as in T3, but teleportation goes to a preference vector v instead of the uniform vector, and the dangling row (Exit) also jumps according to v:

pk+1 = (1 − rho) · pk Pv + rho · v,    Pv = P with the Exit row replaced by v

Three preferences: uniform (1/12 each, the T3 case), the teaching pages 2, 3, 4 (1/3 each) and the research pages 5, 6, 7 (1/3 each). The graph weights are unchanged. Iteration starts at v and stops when the L1 change is below 10−12 (src/bin/B1.rs).

2. What the Preference Changes

  • Where the surfer restarts. With probability 0.10 per step (and from Exit) the walk restarts on the preferred pages, so the scores measure how easily a page is reached from those pages. The ranking becomes "important as seen from the teaching pages" or "from the research pages" instead of "from anywhere".
  • Teaching preference: the course group rises from 0.194 to 0.422; Graphs becomes second, Trees enters the top five, the partner trap shrinks from 0.521 to 0.291 because the walk restarts far from it and needs several steps (through Graphs → Research) to get there.
  • Research preference: the trap grows to 0.577, more than with uniform teleportation, because the research pages are only one or two links away from Partner A (People → Partner A, Updates → Partner A). Home and the course pages get exactly 0: no link path leads from pages 5–8 back to 0–4, and teleportation never lands there.
  • Home is 0 for both personalised versions: it has no incoming links, and only uniform teleportation (or the uniform Exit row of T3) ever placed mass on it.

Why a high score need not mean broad popularity

Partner A has only three incoming links (from People, Updates and its partner page B), yet it is first under all three preferences. Its score comes from the closed loop with Partner B that keeps the walker, and from being close to the restart pages, not from many pages linking to it. Conversely, Courses is linked from Home and Graphs, but with research teleportation its score is 0 because none of those links is ever reached. PageRank answers "where does this particular random surfer spend time", so its value depends on who restarts where.

4. Own Experiment: Which Single Link Best Breaks the Trap?

The course's web_escape adds one link, Partner B → Home. Is that the best possible single link? I tried every new link out of the trap: from Partner A or Partner B to any page they do not link to yet (20 candidates, weight 1 like in web_escape), and recomputed PageRank (rho = 0.10) for all three teleportation preferences. The score is the probability mass left in {9, 10}.

Predictions (written before running)

  1. Links from Partner A will work slightly better than the same links from Partner B, because more mass passes through Partner A.
  2. The best targets are deep inside the course group (Algorithms, Trees): it is farthest from the trap and keeps the walker for a while.
  3. The worst targets are People and Updates, which lead back to Partner A in one step.
  4. The effect will be largest with research teleportation, because the course pages are otherwise empty there.

The "expected steps" column is the mean number of transitions from the target page until the walker first enters {9, 10} under P without teleportation (a 10 × 10 linear system, solved in src/bin/B1_escape.rs). All 60 vectors were checked against NetworkX.

What happened

  • Prediction 1 — right, and stronger than expected. For every target the link from Partner A is better (10 of 10 pairs), and not slightly: Partner A → Courses leaves 0.166, Partner B → Courses 0.196. Almost every walker enters the trap at Partner A (all links into the trap end there; only teleportation can land on B). With the exit at A it can leave at once; with the exit at B it must first spend a step at B, and half the time it is sent back to A instead.
  • Prediction 2 — partly wrong. The best target is Courses, then Algorithms; Trees is only third, about equal to Home. The ranking follows the expected return time almost exactly: Courses 15.7 steps, Algorithms 15.2, Home 14.9, Trees 14.8, Graphs 13.0. Trees is close to the group's only exit (Trees → Graphs has weight 2, and Graphs → Research leaves the group), while Courses sends 3/5 of its walkers to Algorithms, deep inside the group. "Deep" means "far from the exit", not "a page in the middle of the picture".
  • Prediction 3 — right. People (5.2 steps back) and Updates (7.3) are the worst targets; Partner B → People removes the least mass.
  • Prediction 4 — wrong. In relative terms the best link removes about the same share for every preference (68%, 70%, 69%), and the best link is the same, Partner A → Courses, in all three cases. The absolute drop is largest for research teleportation only because that trap was heaviest.
  • Unexpected: a link to Exit is mediocre with uniform teleportation, but with teaching teleportation Partner A → Exit is ranked 2 of 20: Exit's row now sends everything to the teaching pages, so the link acts as a "teleport to the courses".
  • The course's choice Partner B → Home ranks only 9 of 20 (0.201 left). The same target from Partner A would give 0.170, and Partner A → Courses 0.166.

So the best place for a link is where the walker enters the trap, pointing to the page from which the way back is longest. This connects T3 (trapping), B1 (who restarts where) and T2 (the walker's path): the stationary mass in a trap is roughly "how often it is entered × how long one stays", and a single link changes the second factor.

5. Validation

For all three preferences the vectors agree within 10−9 with NetworkX pagerank(web, alpha=0.9, personalization=v, dangling=v, weight="weight") (hw8_check.py), and all are valid distributions. The uniform case equals the T3 result for rho = 0.10.

Bonus B2: Can contracting SCCs preserve maximum flow?

0. Convention

Each strongly connected component is replaced by one vertex. Edges inside a component are dropped; edges between two different components are merged into one edge whose capacity is the sum. The source and sink stay in different components, so the contracted network has a source component and a sink component. SCCs come from the T1 closure (R[i][j] and R[j][i]), the flows from my Edmonds–Karp of T5 (src/bin/B2.rs); NetworkX strongly_connected_components and maximum_flow_value are the second check.

1. Example with an Internal Bottleneck

Edges: s→a (8), s→d (3), a→b (2), b→c (8), c→a (8), c→t (8), d→b (4), d→t (2). SCCs: {s}, {a, b, c}, {d}, {t}.

  • Original: maximum flow 5; minimum cut S = {s, a}, cut edges s -> d (3), a -> b (2).
  • Contracted: maximum flow 10; minimum cut S = {s, abc, d}, cut edges abc -> t (8), d -> t (2).

The internal bottleneck is a → b (capacity 2) inside the component {a, b, c}: everything entering at a must pass it to reach c and then t. The original minimum cut uses it. After contraction a, b and c are one vertex (abc), a → b is an internal edge and disappears, and the network behaves as if flow could move freely inside the component. So the contracted flow is twice as large. Both results were certified with check_flow (flow value = cut capacity in each network).

2. Small Counterexample (for the class comparison)

Edges: s→x (1), x→s (1), x→t (2), with SCCs {s, x}, {t}.

Original flow 1 (cut s -> x (1)); contracted flow 2 (cut sx -> t (2)). Here the source itself shares a component with x (drawn as the vertex sx), and the internal edge s → x is the bottleneck. 3 vertices, 3 edges, total capacity 4, and none of these can be smaller: with 2 vertices s and t are separate single-vertex components and contraction changes nothing; a component with two vertices needs a 2-cycle, plus one edge towards t, so at least 3 edges; and with all capacities 1 both flows are 1, so one capacity must be at least 2.

3. 50 Capacity Variants

The example's topology was kept and every capacity was drawn uniformly from 1 … 10 (SplitMix64, seed 20261026). For each variant both maximum flows were computed in Rust and again with NetworkX.

4. Own Experiment: Exhaustive Search for the Smallest Counterexample

Section 2 argues that 3 vertices, 3 edges and total capacity 4 cannot be beaten. To check this without relying on the argument, src/bin/B2.rs enumerates every simple directed graph (no loops, no parallel edges) on 2, 3 and 4 vertices with s and t fixed and every capacity in a small range, skips graphs where s and t share an SCC, and compares the two maximum flows.

VerticesCapacitiesGraphs checkedSkipped (s, t in one SCC)CounterexamplesSmallest counterexample
21 … 49160—
31 … 38473,249723 edges, capacity 4
41 … 282,477448,96411,1483 edges, capacity 4

With 2 vertices there is no counterexample at all. With 3 vertices the smallest have 3 edges and capacity 4, and there are exactly two: s -> x (1), x -> s (1), x -> t (2); s -> x (2), x -> t (1), t -> x (1). They are mirror images: the component either contains the source (s ⇄ x, internal bottleneck s → x) or the sink (x ⇄ t, bottleneck x → t). The 4-vertex search finds nothing smaller; its smallest examples are the same two graphs with an unused fourth vertex. The 3-vertex enumeration was repeated independently with NetworkX and gives the same counts. Counterexamples are common: 72 of 847 valid 3-vertex graphs and 14% of the 4-vertex ones.

5. Why Contraction Cannot Underestimate

Every s–t cut of the contracted network is also a cut of the original network: put all members of each component on the side of its contracted vertex. The edges crossing it are exactly the original edges between those components, and their capacities were summed, so the two cuts have the same capacity; internal edges never cross because a component is never split. So the contracted minimum cut is the minimum over only some of the original cuts (those that do not split a component), which is ≥ the minimum over all of them. By max-flow = min-cut, contracted max flow ≥ original max flow. The same can be seen with flows: summing the flow on all edges between two components turns any feasible original flow into a feasible contracted flow with the same value. The contracted flow can be larger because the cheapest original cut may have to cut through a component, and that cut no longer exists after contraction.
